xirr-calculator.assumptionNote: XIRR needs at least one outflow and one inflow with valid dates to converge. Cash flows on the same day or all-positive/all-negative series have no solution, and the tool will say so honestly instead of inventing a number.
benefits: The right return metric for real portfolios: SIPs, lumpy investments, and business cash flows.
Matches what Excel's XIRR function gives, without opening a spreadsheet.
Shows your true annualised return including the timing of every deposit.
Instant - paste in dates and amounts and get an answer.

faqs.a: Simple returns ignore timing; XIRR does not. Two investors can both double their money, but the one who did it in 3 years earned far more per year than the one who took 10. XIRR annualises each cash flow by its exact date, so it is the only fair comparison across irregular investments.
faqs.q: Why not just use total return percentage?

faqs.a: IRR assumes regular, evenly spaced cash flows (like annual payments). XIRR handles real-world irregular dates - monthly SIPs, random top-ups, partial withdrawals. If your cash flows are perfectly annual, both give the same answer.
faqs.q: XIRR vs IRR - what is the difference?

faqs.a: Enter outflows (money you invested) as negative and inflows (withdrawals, maturity payouts) as positive. The sign convention is what makes the maths work: the solver finds the rate where discounted inflows exactly balance discounted outflows.
faqs.q: Negative or positive - which sign do I use?

faqs.a: Excel's XIRR uses the same Newton-style solving on the same formula, so results match to the decimal. Tiny differences can appear from day-count conventions (Excel uses 365-day years too) or convergence tolerance.

It can. XIRR assumes interim cash flows are reinvested at the XIRR rate itself, which may be unrealistic. For comparing two investments with similar cash-flow patterns it is excellent; for a single project with wild cash flows, also look at NPV and payback period.

The solver needs at least one negative and one positive cash flow on different dates. Check that your dates are valid, amounts are non-zero, and signs follow the outflow-negative / inflow-positive convention. Also try adding or removing a row - extreme values can break convergence.
faqs.q: Why does it say it could not converge?

xirr-calculator.formula:
XNPV(r) = sum of CF_i / (1 + r)^((d_i - d_0) / 365).
XIRR is the rate r where XNPV(r) = 0.
Solved here with Newton-Raphson iteration from a 10% starting guess.
Example: -10,000 on 2024-01-01, +11,000 on 2025-01-01 -> r ~ 9.97%.

keyFacts: XIRR = Extended Internal Rate of Return: the annualised return for irregularly dated cash flows.
It is the discount rate that makes the net present value of all cash flows exactly zero.
Outflows are negative, inflows are positive - the sign convention is essential.
Excel's XIRR function uses the same maths, so this matches spreadsheet results.
XIRR accounts for the exact timing of every cash flow, unlike simple total return.
It needs at least one inflow and one outflow; otherwise no solution exists.
